title: The Ramgarhia towers
hook: two tall towers built to guard the Harmandir still stand

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bungas: houses round the sacred pool where pilgrims slept and defenders kept watch. Your line was rest by the pool. Who did you offer a place to rest? Today, the bunga that grew upward. Day nine hundred two.

Stand on the marble walkway around the pool at the Harmandir and look up and away from the golden shrine, and two brick towers rise above the rooftops near the edge of the complex. They don't glitter. They aren't covered in gold. They look like what they were: lookouts. Sikh tradition says they belong to the bunga of Jassa Singh Ramgarhia, the carpenter's son this block met earlier. Rest-houses once ringed the pool; this one still stands for people to point to. Today: the Ramgarhia towers.
screen: `TWO BRICK TOWERS ABOVE THE ROOFS.` → `NOT GOLD: LOOKOUTS.` → `JASSA SINGH RAMGARHIA'S BUNGA.`

segments.voice: Start with what a tower is for. A wall keeps people out. A tower lets you see them coming. In years when, as this path has told, armies came to Amritsar more than once, the people who loved the Harmandir needed early warning. From the top of a tower, a watchman could see the roads and fields beyond the city long before anyone at the pool could. So the towers are about attention. Somebody climbs up, and stays up, and looks, while others below bathe and pray and sleep. Guarding, in this picture, is mostly patience. Hours of nothing, for the one moment that matters. Now notice who built them. Jassa Singh Ramgarhia came, tradition says, from a carpenter's family, a family of builders. His band's gift to the Harmandir was not mainly gold or a donation. It was a building, made to protect someone else's prayers. A builder guarding with what he knew how to build. And third, notice the word still. The towers stand. Much of what stood round the pool in the misl years has been rebuilt or cleared, but these lookouts remain, and pilgrims walk past them on their way to the shrine. They no longer need watchmen in the old way. They've become a kind of sign: a sacred place is something people have chosen to guard. The Harmandir sits low, at the level of the water, with doors open on every side. In Sikh telling, those open doors are a welcome to all. And just beyond the edge of that openness, someone once built towers so the welcome could keep going. Guarding towers.
screen: `A TOWER LETS YOU SEE THEM COMING.` · `GUARDING IS MOSTLY PATIENCE.` · `A BUILDER'S GIFT.` · `STILL STANDING BY THE POOL.` · then, large: `GUARDING TOWERS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes standing guard. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing that's precious to you and easy to lose: your kids' bedtime, a friendship you've neglected, a quiet morning hour, your own health, the trust someone has put in you. Now take the watchman's post. Ask what's coming down the road toward it: a busy month, a habit, a screen, a resentment. You don't have to fight anything yet. Just see it coming. Decide one small way to keep watch. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
bunga, a rest-house near the Harmandir; the Ramgarhia towers are the two lookouts of Jassa Singh Ramgarhia's bunga, built to guard the shrine, still standing near the sacred pool. Today's word.
Your line: guarding towers. Today, stand guard over one precious thing. Protect an hour, a promise, or a person, and don't let the day take it. Day nine hundred two.

howItsDone: Pilgrims at the Harmandir Sahib complex in Amritsar can see the towers of the Ramgarhia Bunga near the edge of the precinct, and Sikh histories remember Jassa Singh Ramgarhia as their builder.
